{{Short description|Mathematical equation}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Weyl's lemma''', named after [[Hermann Weyl]], states that every [[weak solution]] of [[Laplace's equation]] is a [[smooth function|smooth]] solution. This contrasts with the [[wave equation]], for example, which has weak solutions that are not smooth solutions. Weyl's lemma is a special case of [[elliptic PDE|elliptic]] or [[hypoelliptic| hypoelliptic regularity]].

==Statement of the lemma==
Let <math>\Omega</math> be an [[open set|open subset]] of <math>n</math>-dimensional Euclidean space <math>\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>, and let <math>\Delta</math> denote the usual [[Laplace operator]]. Weyl's lemma<ref>[[Hermann Weyl]], The method of orthogonal projections in potential theory, ''Duke Math. J.'', 7, 411–444 (1940). See Lemma 2, p. 415</ref> states that if a [[locally integrable]] function <math>u \in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1}(\Omega)</math> is a weak solution of Laplace's equation, in the sense that

:<math>\int_\Omega u(x) \, \Delta \varphi (x) \, dx = 0</math> 

for every [[Spaces of test functions and distributions|test function]] ([[smooth function|smooth]] function with [[compact support]]) <math>\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Omega)</math>, then (up to redefinition on a set of [[measure zero]]) <math>u \in C^{\infty}(\Omega)</math> is smooth and satisfies <math>\Delta u = 0</math> pointwise in <math>\Omega</math>.

This result implies the interior regularity of [[harmonic function]]s in <math>\Omega</math>, but it does not say anything about their regularity on the boundary <math>\partial\Omega</math>.

== Idea of the proof ==
To prove Weyl's lemma, one [[Convolution|convolves]] the function <math>u</math> with an appropriate [[mollifier]] <math>\varphi_\varepsilon</math> and shows that the mollification <math>u_\varepsilon = \varphi_\varepsilon\ast u</math> satisfies Laplace's equation, which implies that <math>u_\varepsilon</math> has the mean value property. Taking the limit as <math>\varepsilon\to 0</math> and using the properties of mollifiers, one finds that <math>u</math> also has the mean value property,<ref>The mean value property is known to characterize [[harmonic function]]s in the following sense. Let <math>h \in \mathrm{C}(\Omega)</math>. Then <math>h</math> is [[harmonic function|harmonic]] in the usual sense (so <math>h \in \mathrm{C}^2(\Omega)</math> and <math>\left.\Delta h=0\right)</math> if and only if for all balls <math>B_r\left(x_0\right) \Subset \Omega</math> we have
:<math>
h\left(x_0\right)=\frac{1}{\omega_{n-1} r^{n-1}} \int_{\partial B_r\left(x_0\right)} h(x) \mathrm{d} S_x .
</math>
where <math>\omega_{n-1} r^{n-1}</math> is the (''n'' &minus; 1)-dimensional area of the hypersphere <math>\partial B_r\left(x_0\right)</math>.

Using polar coordinates about <math>x_0</math> we see that when <math>h</math> is [[harmonic function|harmonic]], then for <math>B_r\left(x_0\right) \Subset \Omega</math>,
:<math>
h\left(x_0\right)=\left(\rho_r * h\right)\left(x_0\right) .
</math></ref> which implies that it is a smooth solution of Laplace's equation.<ref>Bernard Dacorogna, ''Introduction to the Calculus of Variations,'' 2nd ed., Imperial College Press (2009), p. 148.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://math.mit.edu/~dws/boulder/weyl.pdf |title=Weyl’s lemma, one of many |last=Stroock |first=Daniel W.}}</ref> Alternative proofs use the smoothness of the fundamental solution of the Laplacian or suitable a priori elliptic estimates.
{{Math proof|
Let <math>\left(\rho_{\varepsilon}\right)_{\varepsilon>0}</math> be the standard [[mollifier]].

Fix a compact set <math>\Omega^{\prime} \Subset \Omega</math> and put <math>\varepsilon_0=\operatorname{dist}\left(\Omega^{\prime}, \partial \Omega\right)</math> be the distance between <math>\Omega^{\prime}</math> and the boundary of <math>\Omega</math>.

For each <math>x \in \Omega^{\prime}</math> and <math>\varepsilon \in\left(0, \varepsilon_0\right)</math> the function
:<math>
y \longmapsto \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)
</math>
belongs to [[Spaces of test functions and distributions|test functions]] <math>\mathcal{D}(\Omega)</math> and so we may consider
:<math>\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle</math>
We assert that it is independent of <math>\varepsilon \in\left(0, \varepsilon_0\right)</math>. To prove it we calculate <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon} \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)</math> for <math>x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n</math>.

Recall that
:<math>
\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)=\varepsilon^{-n} \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)
</math>
where the standard mollifier kernel <math>\rho</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> was defined at [[Mollifier#Concrete_example]]. If we put
:<math>
\theta(t)= \begin{cases}\frac{1}{c_n} \mathrm{e}^{\frac{1}{t-1}} & \text { if } t<1, \\ 0 & \text { if } t \geqslant 1,\end{cases}
</math>
then <math>\rho(x)=\theta\left(|x|^2\right)</math>.

Clearly <math>\theta \in \mathrm{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})</math> satisfies <math>\theta(t)=0</math> for <math>t \geqslant 1</math>. Now calculate
:<math>
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}\left(\varepsilon^{-n} \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) & =-n \varepsilon^{-n-1} \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)-\varepsilon^{-n} \nabla \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right) \cdot \frac{x-y}{\varepsilon^2} \\
& =-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{n+1}}\left(n \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)+\nabla \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right) \cdot \frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)
\end{aligned}
</math>
Put <math>K(x)=-n \rho(x)-\nabla \rho(x) \cdot x</math> so that
:<math>
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}\left(\varepsilon^{-n} \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{n+1}} K\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right) .
</math>
In terms of <math>\rho(x)=\theta\left(|x|^2\right)</math> we get
:<math>
K(x)=-\operatorname{div}(\rho(x) x)=-\operatorname{div}\left(\theta\left(|x|^2\right) x\right)
</math>
and if we set
:<math>
\Theta(t)=\frac{1}{2} \int_t^{\infty} \theta(s) \mathrm{d} s
</math>
then <math>\Theta \in \mathrm{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})</math> with <math>\Theta(t)=0</math> for <math>t \geqslant 1</math>, and <math>\Theta^{\prime}(t)=-\frac{1}{2} \theta(t)</math>. Consequently
:<math>
-\theta\left(|x|^2\right) x=\nabla\left(\Theta\left(|x|^2\right)\right)
</math>
and so <math>K(x)=\operatorname{div} \nabla\left(\Theta\left(|x|^2\right)\right)=(\Delta \Phi)(x)</math>, where <math>\Phi(x)=\Theta\left(|x|^2\right)</math>. Observe that <math>\Phi \in \mathcal{D}\left(\overline{B_1(0)}\right)</math>, and
:<math>
\begin{aligned}
-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{n+1}}\left(n \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)+\nabla \rho\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right) \cdot \frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right) & =\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{n+1}} \Delta_y\left(\Phi\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) \\
& =\Delta_y\left(\varepsilon^{1-n} \Phi\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) .
\end{aligned}
</math>
Here <math>y \mapsto \varepsilon^{1-n} \Phi\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)</math> is supported in <math>\overline{B_{\varepsilon}(x)} \subset \Omega</math>, and so by assumption
:<math>\left\langle u, \Delta_y\left(\varepsilon^{1-n} \Phi\left(\frac{x-y}{\varepsilon}\right)\right)\right\rangle=0</math>.
Now by considering difference quotients we see that
:<math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle=\left\langle u, \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon} \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle</math>.
Indeed, for <math>\varepsilon, \varepsilon^{\prime}>0</math> we have
:<math>\begin{aligned}
\frac{\rho_{\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{\prime}}(x-y)-\rho_{\varepsilon}(x-y)}{\varepsilon^{\prime}} & \stackrel{\mathrm{FTC}}{=} \int_0^1 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \rho_{\varepsilon+t \varepsilon^{\prime}}(x-y) \mathrm{d} t \\
& \left.\underset{\varepsilon^{\prime} \searrow0}{\longrightarrow} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\right|_{s=\varepsilon} \rho_s(x-y)
\end{aligned}</math>
in <math>\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\Omega)</math> with respect to <math>y</math>, provided <math>x \in \Omega^{\prime}</math> and <math>0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0</math> (since we may differentiate both sides with respect to <math>y)</math>. But then <math>\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle=0</math>, and so <math>\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle=\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon_1}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle</math> for all <math>\varepsilon \in\left(0, \varepsilon_0\right)</math>, where <math>\varepsilon_1 \in\left(0, \varepsilon_0\right)</math>. Now let <math>\varphi \in \mathcal{D}\left(\Omega^{\prime}\right)</math>. Then, by the usual trick when convolving distributions with [[Spaces of test functions and distributions|test functions]],
:<math>\begin{aligned}
\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle \varphi(x) \mathrm{d} x & =\left\langle u, \int_{\Omega^{\prime}} \rho_{\varepsilon}(x-\cdot) \varphi(x) \mathrm{d} x\right\rangle \\
& =\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon} * \varphi\right\rangle
\end{aligned}</math>
and so for <math>\varepsilon \in\left(0, \varepsilon_1\right)</math> we have
:<math>\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon} * \varphi\right\rangle=\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon_1}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle \varphi(x) \mathrm{d} x</math>.
Hence, as <math>\rho_{\varepsilon} * \varphi \rightarrow \varphi</math> in <math>\mathcal{D}(\Omega)</math> as <math>\varepsilon \searrow 0</math>, we get
:<math>\langle u, \varphi\rangle=\int_{\Omega^{\prime}}\left\langle u, \rho_{\varepsilon_1}(x-\cdot)\right\rangle \varphi(x) \mathrm{d} x</math>.
Consequently <math>\left.u\right|_{\Omega^{\prime}} \in \mathrm{C}^{\infty}\left(\Omega^{\prime}\right)</math>, and since <math>\Omega^{\prime}</math> was arbitrary, we are done.
}}

== Generalization to distributions ==
More generally, the same result holds for every [[Distribution (mathematics) | distributional solution]] of Laplace's equation: If <math>T\in D'(\Omega)</math> satisfies <math>\langle T, \Delta \varphi\rangle = 0</math> for every <math>\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)</math>, then <math>T</math> is a regular distribution associated with a smooth solution <math>u\in C^\infty(\Omega)</math> of Laplace's equation.<ref>[[Lars Gårding]], ''Some Points of Analysis and their History'', AMS (1997), p. 66.</ref>

== Connection with hypoellipticity ==
Weyl's lemma follows from more general results concerning the regularity properties of elliptic or hypoelliptic operators.<ref>[[Lars Hörmander]], ''The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I'', 2nd ed., Springer-Verlag (1990), p.110</ref> A linear partial differential operator <math>P</math> with smooth coefficients is hypoelliptic if the [[support (mathematics) | singular support]] of <math>P u</math> is equal to the singular support of <math>u</math> for every distribution <math>u</math>. The Laplace operator is hypoelliptic, so if <math>\Delta u = 0</math>, then the singular support of <math>u</math> is empty since the singular support of <math>0</math> is empty, meaning that <math>u\in C^\infty(\Omega)</math>. In fact, since the Laplacian is elliptic, a stronger result is true, and solutions of  <math>\Delta u = 0</math> are [[analytic function | real-analytic]].
